headline: Musk admits he throttled Ukraine's Starlink, France counts almost 1,000 arrests as protests spread across Europe, and Brazil votes in a dead-heat runoff

stories.title: Musk says SpaceX throttled Ukraine's Starlink over "offensive drone strikes"
facts: Hours after Kyiv said service was back to full speed, Musk posted that Ukraine's military "used it for offensive drone strikes to kill people. That loophole was closed last week."
He also said Starshield, the military version, "is controlled by the US government".
Since 14 October, drones flying faster than about 100 mph lost their link; Ukraine's defence ministry now records stable connections above 400 km/h.
Musk added that without Starlink "the Ukrainian front line would collapse immediately", calling it "NOT a threat".
A Ukrainian presidential adviser said Ukraine is "physically unable" to use Starlink for long- and medium-range attack drones.
stories.whyItMatters: Musk is now openly defending the slowdown, which shows one company can switch off a core part of Ukraine's front-line drone network.

image.alt: A man, with at least three blankets around him and a drink in his hand, sits on a chair on the side of a street. Next to him is a small picnic table with a starlink terminal on it.

stories.title: France: almost 1,000 arrests after another protest Saturday, and unrest spreads across Europe
facts: Interior minister Laurent Nuñez put arrests at almost 1,000 and expects the number to rise. Last weekend's total was about 2,700.
The ministry counted 410,000 marchers nationwide and the CGT union about 800,000. In Paris the counts were 110,000 and 250,000.
Daytime marches were largely peaceful. Late clashes brought tear gas and water cannon in Paris, burning barricades in Marseille, and a shop broken into in Bordeaux.
Barcelona saw more than 100 arrests. Milan deployed 500 soldiers alongside 5,000 police, police in Rome used tear gas, and Tirana, Brussels and Lisbon also had protests.
Around 13,000 people rallied peacefully against the RN congress in Orléans.
stories.whyItMatters: There was far less looting than last weekend, but the cost-of-living anger is now spreading across Europe instead of fading.

image.alt: People clash with police officers as objects burn at a barricade during a demonstration against the high cost of living in Bordeaux, France.

stories.title: Brazil votes today: Flávio Bolsonaro edges Lula 51–49 in final polls
facts: Datafolha, Quaest and PoderData all show Flávio Bolsonaro at 51% of valid votes to Lula's 49%. That's within the margin of error.
In the first round, Flávio took 47.03% and Lula 45.16%.
Lula, 80, is seeking an unprecedented fourth term. His rival is a son of former president Jair Bolsonaro.
stories.whyItMatters: Brazil is Latin America's largest democracy, and the result lands tonight Berlin time.

image.alt: A stylised map of Brazil shaded in a red-to-blue gradient, beside the words "Brazil election results".

stories.title: Ten days out: Obama hits the trail, and Trump unveils Audi's first US plant at a rally
facts: In Ohio and Detroit, Obama said: "We have never seen a president excel in straight-up grifting on your dime like this."
At a Perry, Georgia rally, Trump announced the carmaker's first US factory.
Audi says it will invest about $4 billion and create about 4,500 jobs. The plant is designed for up to 200,000 SUVs a year, with construction from 2027 and production in the early 2030s.
stories.whyItMatters: It's a German carmaker's answer to US tariffs, announced as a campaign moment.

image.alt: Audi in the United States - Audi aims to further strengthen its position in the U.S. market. The new Audi Q9 is specifically tailored to the needs of American customers.

stories.title: Israel will seal the West Bank on election day; Houthis claim strikes on Saudi oil sites
facts: Israel says it will close all West Bank land crossings on 27 October, election day, and bar Palestinian workers from settlements.
This follows a Hebron-area operation of arrests and demolitions after a checkpoint attack killed two soldiers.
Protesters again rallied in Tel Aviv against Netanyahu over his role in 7 October.
Yemen's Houthis claimed attacks on Saudi oil sites, airports and military targets. Missiles hit coastguard facilities in Aden, and Saudi Arabia reported debris near Mecca and Medina.

image.alt: An Israeli army vehicle passes near the closed entrance of Hebron, in the Israeli-occupied West Bank

stories.title: C++26 fails its ISO ballot
facts: Robert Seacord reports that 9 of 22 national bodies voted no on the C++26 draft international standard. The limit is 25%.
Individual experts voted 12 of 20 yes, which is 60% against the 66.66% needed.
ISO's project record moved the draft to stage 40.60 on 24 October.
Contracts were the main sticking point. The committee's March vote to finalise C++26 was 114–12–3, and Herb Sutter said the no votes were mostly about contracts.
Neither WG21 nor ISO has said what happens next.
stories.whyItMatters: The language's next standard is now in limbo, and contracts are likely to be the fight over any revised draft.
